record.tranche_reason: Tests how regularization affects superposition in toy autoencoders, using feature representations and geometric measures rather than the original sources’ neuron-response methods.
record.gate_note: The study reports toy-model results on feature superposition, representation geometry, and reconstruction performance. It does not test real vision or language neurons. Background claims and figures from cited work are not study results; chart values not stated in the text are not inferred.
record.test_reason: Toy ReLU autoencoders with dropout on the hidden layer, which gives the neurons a privileged basis. The study measures how much features are packed onto neurons across sparsity levels, with and without dropout, along with reconstruction cost. This bears on V5 (regularization changes polysemanticity, at a cost) and weakly on V3 (sparsity drives packing onto neurons). No real vision or language model neurons are measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Dropout generally inhibits superposition in toy autoencoders, except with varying feature importance and low sparsity. There is a performance tradeoff. The proposed explanations are speculative.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the Anthropic toy-autoencoder setup with dropout added, rather than measuring neuron responses in the original sources’ vision models. The study measures toy feature embeddings, weight geometry, and reconstruction performance.
record.method_sensitivity: The effect differs with sparsity and whether feature importance is uniform or varies; dropout probability also affects the reported tradeoff, with p=0.4 described as aggressive and p=0.15 as intermediate.

fits_no_version.finding: In the vanilla toy autoencoder (no privileged basis), feature superposition rises with sparsity, from 2 orthogonal features to a 5-feature pentagon.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse features are packed into fewer latent dimensions as sparsity increases (feature superposition, without reference to neurons).

record.problems: The evidence is from small synthetic toy autoencoders, not real-world networks. Exact chart values and uncertainty estimates are not stated in the text. The authors note that the dimensions-per-feature metric gives a result in the no-sparsity case that conflicts with the bar-chart interpretation, and their explanation is speculative.
record.rows_left_out: No reported results relevant to the tested versions were left out. Numeric values shown only in figures were not transcribed because the text does not state them.

untested.parts: Does not show that superposition explains polysemantic neurons in trained real networks. The feature-to-neuron ratio is not varied.
No tests of initialization, noise, or the case with enough neurons for every feature.
No activation-function or architecture comparisons. No real-world models. The size of the performance loss is not quantified.
Activation-range and explanation-scoring choices are not tested. The study only notes that the dims-per-feature metric conflicts with the bar charts.

missing.what: A no-dropout model trained only to the dropout model's performance (0.05 MSE) still shows much more superposition. So dropout's reduction is not just an artifact of worse performance.
missing.locator: Results, figure 'superposition visualisation for dropout p=0, trained to 0.05 mse loss'

record.verdict_notes: LessWrong hackathon post with no numbers or uncertainty in the text; all results are read from figures as described in the prose. Neither original source applies here. The basis is privileged only in the dropout models, so only those rows speak to polysemantic neurons as such.

versions.untested_parts: No image classifier or vision-model neurons are tested.
No transformer language models, tokens, or language contexts are tested.
Tests superposition in toy autoencoders, but does not establish that this mechanism explains polysemantic neurons in trained real-world networks or vary feature-to-dimension capacity independently.
Does not test initialization, training noise, or polysemanticity when there is enough capacity for every feature.
Tests dropout in toy autoencoders only; does not compare activation functions or modern architectures, and does not quantify whether the performance cost is large.
Does not examine whether mixed real-world neuron responses share a feature.
Notes a discrepancy between a dimensions-per-feature metric and bar-chart interpretation, but does not test activation-range or explanation-scoring choices.

rows.subject: toy model autoencoder
rows.operation_detail: Trained with dropout and compared learned feature embeddings with the no-dropout model.
rows.measure: Feature embedding geometry / extent of superposition
rows.baseline: Without dropout, the sparsest case represents all 5 features in a regular pentagon.
rows.value: With dropout, superposition still increases with sparsity, but the model never goes beyond antipodal pairs and never represents all 5 features.
rows.note: The text also says the features become basis-aligned with the neurons.
rows.check: For V5, dropout clearly lowers superposition (no pentagon, at most antipodal pairs). For V3, within the basis-aligned dropout model, packing onto neurons still rises with sparsity. 'Partial' understated both effects.

source_check.notes: Informal LessWrong post with figures only and no numbers. The dropout p for the 20-feature runs is not stated; p=0.4 is likely but only inferred. The hidden layer is linear plus dropout, and dropout supplies the privileged basis. A no-dropout model trained to the same loss still shows much more superposition.

statements.correction: lw:znShP model: h=dropout(Wx), x'=ReLU(W^T h+b). There is no hidden-layer nonlinearity. Dropout induces the privileged basis, so features become basis-aligned with neurons. At p=0.4, 5 features in 2 dims, superposition still rises with sparsity but never goes beyond antipodal pairs.
statements.problem: This study is grouped under 'toy ReLU networks with a hidden-layer nonlinearity' and 'Toy ReLU hidden-layer models'. But the post's hidden layer is linear with dropout. ReLU is only on the output. The sentence about lw:znShP itself is correct.
